summary: Suggests a mail mapping between X.400 (1988) or ISO 10021 messages and RFC 822 messages, for the Internet and UK Academic communities. It is experimental and not a standard. It updates RFCs 822, 987, and 1026. It was replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

plainLanguage.summary: Two mail systems use different formats. This is a translation guide so a letter from one can be read by the other.

questions: how to gateway x.400 and internet mail

subtitle: A rulebook for gateways that translate mail between X.400 (1988) systems and Internet RFC 822 mail.

tldr.problem: Users of RFC 822 mail and users of X.400 (1988) messaging needed to exchange messages, and different gateways needed to translate in the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps each service and header between the two systems, defines a text form for X.400 O/R addresses and a way to carry RFC 822 addresses inside X.400, and keeps the mapping reversible so information is not lost.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1138 is Experimental, not a standard. It has been replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156 and was updated by RFC 1148.

today: RFC 1138 is Experimental and has been replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156. It was updated by RFC 1148, and it updated RFC 822, RFC 987 and RFC 1026.

sections.title: Purpose and General Approach
sections.content:
RFC 1138 is a memo that suggests an electronic mail protocol mapping for the Internet community and the UK Academic Community and asks for discussion. It does not specify an Internet standard. It maps between the CCITT X.400 (1988) Recommendations, also known as ISO IEC 10021 or MOTIS, and the RFC 822 mail protocol and protocols derived from it. The mapping aims to need no changes to end systems.

The text builds on RFC 987 and RFC 1026, which did a similar mapping for X.400 (1984). It does not obsolete them because its domain is different: the mapping targets the full 1988 version of X.400, and a message headed for a 1984 system should still use RFC 987.

The RFC states its principles as goals. The mapping should be pragmatic, functionality across the gateway should be as high as possible, information should not be lost, and the specification should be reversible, so that a double transformation returns you to the start. Subsetting is strongly discouraged. The document warns that the rest of it is technically detailed and only makes sense to readers who know RFC 822 and X.400 (1988).
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is a fair translator that does not leave out words and can translate back to the original.

sections.title: Which Services Cross the Gateway
sections.content:
The gateway model treats X.400 as an Interpersonal Messaging System (IPMS) with two main objects, the IPM (message) and the IPN (receipt notification). RFC 822 is treated as a message plus an underlying 822-MTS that names recipients and an error return address. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a message always becomes an IPM. Going the other way, an RFC 822 message can come from a report, an IPN or an IPM.

Chapter 2 goes through each service and labels it Supported, Partially Supported, Not Supported or Not Applicable. Basic fields such as From:, To:, Cc:, Subject: and Message-Id: are supported. Keywords:, Encrypted: and Resent-* are carried in an IPM heading extension, and Comments: becomes an extra body part.

X.400 services that RFC 822 cannot express get new RFC 822 header fields, for example Importance:, Sensitivity:, Expiry-Date:, Language:, X400-Recipients: and X400-MTS-Identifier:. Services like content confidentiality and message security labelling are not supported. Where an unsupported element is marked critical, a non-delivery notification is generated; otherwise the request is ignored. A message passing through several gateways is expected to end up at about the level of RFC 822 services.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of a letter have an obvious home on the other side. Others get put in a special box or a note on the outside, and a few cannot be carried at all.

sections.title: Basic Encodings Between ASCII and X.400
sections.content:
X.400 is encoded with ASN.1 while RFC 822 is text, so Chapter 3 defines text forms for the ASN.1 types the mapping needs, including Boolean, NumericString, PrintableString, T.61 strings, UTCTime, Integer and Object Identifier. A gateway treats all IA5 as ASCII. Teletex characters are written as three-digit decimal octets in braces.

A key trick is encoding ASCII inside a PrintableString, which lacks characters common in RFC 822 addresses. Special codes stand in for them: (a) for @, (p) for %, (b) for !, (q) for a double quote, (u) for an underscore, (l) and (r) for round brackets, and ( followed by three digits ) for any other ASCII character. For example, foo(a)bar maps to foo@bar.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope on one side has no @ sign key, so it is written as (a). Both sides agree on the secret spelling.

sections.title: Mapping Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC calls addressing probably the trickiest problem for a gateway. An X.400 O/R address is a set of attribute-value pairs such as Country (C), administration domain (ADMD), private domain (PRMD), organization (O), organizational unit (OU) and personal name (PN). Chapter 4 defines a text form for it, such as /I=J/S=Linnimouth/GQ=5/@Marketing.Widget.COM.

An X.400 address can be encoded in an RFC 822 address in two ways. The domain part can be associated through mapping tables with the higher levels of the O/R hierarchy. For example, AC.UK might be associated with C=GB, ADMD=GOLD 400 and PRMD=UK.AC. The remaining attributes go in the local part. A simple personal name can be written like J.Linnimouth or Marshall.Rose.

In the other direction, a genuine RFC 822 address is carried in X.400 using a domain defined attribute of type RFC-822, with the address as a PrintableString (for example Postel(a)venera.isi.edu). If the value is too long for the domain-defined attribute (maximum length 128), the gateway should reject the message at the MTS level. The mapping tables use the longest match, and Appendix F gives their format. Source routing through the encoding is strongly discouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: An address on one side is a list of boxes (country, company, person). On the other side it is one line with dots. The rules say how to turn one into the other, and back.

sections.title: Detailed Mappings of Messages and Reports
sections.content:
Going from RFC 822 to X.400, one IP Message is generated, with the RFC 822 headers going into the IPM heading and the body becoming one IA5 body part. To: maps to the primary recipients, Cc: to the copy recipients, Bcc: to the blind copy recipients, Reply-To: to the reply recipients, and Subject: to the subject. If a Sender: is present, From: maps to the authorizing users. Fields with no home go in an extension that holds the full header text. Upper-bound handling has three allowed options: ignore bounds, reject, or truncate.

Going from X.400 to RFC 822, a single RFC 822 message is made from an IP Message, a report or a notification. Body parts become a single body. X.400 services without an RFC 822 equivalent become new header fields.

Return of contents is handled in one of two ways, depending on how widely the X.400 community supports it. Where it is not widely supported, the gateway does not request content return, always requests a report, and creates its own useful report or a timeout failure notice for the RFC 822 originator. Probes are answered by the gateway itself. The RFC gives an example delivery report with a Message-Type of Delivery Report.

Appendices cover differences from RFC 987, details for JNT Mail and UUCP mail, an object identifier, the BNF summary and the format of address mapping tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of the letter has a spot to go in on the other side. If there is no spot, the translator writes it on an extra label so nothing is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that security issues are not discussed in the memo. In the service tables, the X.400 security services, such as content confidentiality, content integrity and message security labelling, are listed as not supported across the gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator book does not say how to keep letters secret. The secret-letter features of one side just do not cross over.
